chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
title: His father's advice to make music a business
summary: His father told him to treat music as a business rather than fun, a worry rooted in his struggles to collect money on his newspaper route.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, I just wanted to ask you about your father, you know, because when you did go to junior college, I guess he was paying for that, wasn't he?
Oh, yes, he was.
But you didn't get a chance to actually graduate that time, did you?
No, I didn't.
So then, did he eventually get to be satisfied that you were playing piano and everything, Was he content?

Well, I'll tell you what he did. He finally talked to me. He said, "I'll tell you what. Now, listen. Now, I don't think too much of this business, you playing, you know, playing for all this --" this is just what he called it --"playing for all this butt-shaking." He said, "But let me tell you something. Now, one of the worst things that can

happen is to get carried away behind a whole lot of butt-shaking because there's nothing happening. That's all there is. I just hope you don't get to the point where you think that's all there is happening." He says, "I want you to make a business out of it."
Oh, yes.

He says, "Whatever -- if you're going to play music, do it as a business, not as a fun." He says, "Don't get carried away with the fun that goes along with it, because a lot of people get carried away with the fun, they never go no further than that. It's just fun from now on." And he says --
How did he know that?
How did he know that?
I mean, that's perfectly true, isn't it?
I don't know how he knew that, but I guess he always thought that I would get carried away and forget about all the business ends.
Well, I mean, it's true, but for many people, the life is just as important as the music.
Well, that's true.
I mean, they like -- I mean, even the one(s) (inaudible), don't they?
But you know, I did notice this

though, when I was coming up as a kid, I used to sell papers, you know, how you sell them a weekly paper or whatever it was, you know? And I would -- oh, I'd -- I could get out there and just throw them papers and get rid of them, get that part of it done. But he would have to lay on me and make me go collect that money. And I think that's the reason that he figured that I would always be the type would get out there and get carried away and have no business sense at all about it.

And I was glad that he did. I could see it later on, you know, in life. Because I would. I would work like everything selling those papers and -- but a lot of people, he says, "Okay, now, how many have paid you?" Then I'd go back over my books and then I hated to have to walk maybe eight or ten miles to collect that money. You know? And I said, "Well, I'll catch them next week." "Next week? It's going to be double next week."
That's right.

He said, "Get it right now." And I'd get so mad I didn't know what to do. Oh, I would get mad, you know? But see, I did a lot of walking as a kid coming up, you know, because when I came up, that's the only way you could get to where you had to go. Everything was walk.
